text.p: This is how major world bond markets were trading in late European business on Monday.

GERMANY - The debt market ended trade slightly easier and dealers said the lack of new factors to drive the market combined with the U.S. holiday to consign trade to narrow ranges. The December Bund future on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) was trading at 99.31, up 0.04 from Friday's settlement price.

BRITAIN - Gilts hovered around Friday's close for most of the day after an initial dip on higher than expected September output prices. Further digestion of the figures allayed any inflationary fears as core output prices rose at their slowest rate in nearly 30 years. The December long gilt future on LIFFE was trading at 110-11/32, up 1/32 from Friday's settlement price.

FRANCE - The December bond future lost more ground but pulled above support levels in the closing minutes on MATIF in a further correction which set in last Friday after a tearway week for French assets. The December notional bond future on the MATIF in Paris settled at 125.94, down 0.26 from Friday's settlement price.

ITALY - Bond futures held to lower level in late afternoon with operators taking profits after the lira showed a slightly easier tone. The December bond future on LIFFE was trading at 122.90, down 0.38 from Friday's settlement price.
UNITED STATES - The U.S. Treasury market was closed for the U.S. Columbus holiday. The market will open again on Tuesday.

JAPAN - The key December Japanese government bond futures contract dropped to close below 123 on Monday for the first time in more than a week, with its seven-day rally corrected by profit-taking. In after hours trading the December future on LIFFE was trading at 122.92, down 0.38 from Friday's settlement price on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

EUROBONDS - Mainstream activity was slow with activity centered on peripheral currencies. The popular lira sector saw further issuance with a 600 billion lire zero-coupon bond from Cariplo and a 200 billion lire six-year straight from KfW. The rand sector was reawakened after a four-month sleep but the 100 million rand EIB bond was not universally well-received. Two Kiwi dollar bonds were launched following recent New Zealand elections.
